nameStory: The watermelon gets its name from being, quite literally, a melon full of water! This juicy fruit is about 92% water, making it nature's own hydration station. The name perfectly captures what makes this fruit so refreshing on hot summer days.
description: Watermelon is a sprawling vine with deeply lobed, pale green leaves that feels rough and sandpapery to the touch. The plant produces bright yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers and sends out long trailing stems that can stretch 10-15 feet across the ground. While originally from Africa, watermelons are now grown in gardens and farms throughout New England during our warm summer months, producing the familiar large, striped green fruits we love.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided into 3-5 rounded lobes with a rough, sandpaper-like texture that feels scratchy when you run your fingers across the surface

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow, funnel-shaped flowers about 1 inch across with 5 petals that open in the morning and have a faint, sweet scent

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Long, trailing vines that sprawl along the ground with curly, spring-like tendrils that grab onto nearby objects for support

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, hollow stems covered in short, stiff hairs that feel prickly to the touch and branch out from a central root system

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Large, round to oval green fruits with dark stripes that make a hollow 'thump' sound when tapped and have a smooth, waxy skin

habitat: Watermelons are cultivated plants found in home gardens, community gardens, and farms throughout New England. They need full sun, well-drained sandy or loamy soil, and plenty of space to spread their long vines. You'll typically see them growing in raised beds or dedicated melon patches where they have room to ramble.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are planted after the last frost when soil is warm, usually late May in New England. Young seedlings emerge with their first rounded seed leaves.
seasonality.summer: Vines spread rapidly and produce yellow flowers in July, followed by developing fruits. This is when the distinctive lobed leaves and trailing growth habit are most obvious.
seasonality.fall: Fruits ripen in late summer to early fall, turning from pale to dark green with prominent stripes. Vines begin to yellow and die back with first frost.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground growth survives New England winters. Plants are completely dormant and must be replanted each year from seed.

funFact: Watermelon rinds can actually explode! In Japan, farmers sometimes wrap rubber bands around growing watermelons just to watch the pressure build up until the fruit literally bursts apart in a spectacular green explosion.
confusionNotes: Young watermelon vines might be confused with cucumber or squash plants, but watermelon leaves are much more deeply lobed and feel noticeably rougher and more sandpapery than the smoother leaves of cucumbers or the broader, less-divided leaves of most squashes.
contextualKnowledge: While we think of watermelons as sweet treats, they're botanically fruits but culinarily often treated as vegetables in some cultures. The white rind is edible and commonly pickled or stir-fried in many countries, though most Americans only eat the red flesh.
compareHints: Watermelon is the only member of its genus commonly grown in New England. Within the gourd family, it's distinguished from cucumbers by its much more deeply divided, rougher leaves, from summer squash by its trailing (not bushy) growth habit, and from winter squash and pumpkins by its less heart-shaped, more finely divided foliage and distinctive sandpaper-rough leaf texture.
